At the start of a month she borrowed Rs 20,000 at 12 per cent simple interest per annum for 6 months and spent the entire amount on 400 identical notebooks. She marked each notebook at 40 per cent above its cost price. During the month she sold 200 notebooks at a discount of 10 per cent on the marked price and the remaining 200 notebooks at the marked price. In the following month she bought the same notebooks again at the same cost, raised the marked price by 10 per cent over the earlier marked price, and then announced a festival discount of 10 per cent on the new marked price.

rows.subject: gat
rows.body: What is the smallest number greater than 100 that leaves a remainder of 3 when divided by 6, by 8 and by 10?
rows.explanation: Numbers leaving remainder 3 with all three divisors are of the form (LCM of 6, 8 and 10) x k + 3. The LCM is 120, so the numbers are 3, 123, 243 and so on, and the smallest above 100 is 123. The LCM itself, 120, leaves remainder 0, and 117 leaves remainder 5 with 8.
tags: ncert:CUET GAT syllabus, Quantitative Reasoning: number system, LCM and a common remainder

rows.subject: gat
rows.body: Six workers can finish a job in 20 days. After 5 days, 3 more workers join them, all working at the same rate. In how many days from the start is the job finished?
rows.explanation: The job is 6 x 20 = 120 worker-days. In 5 days the 6 workers do 30 worker-days, leaving 90, which 9 workers finish in 10 days, so the total is 5 + 10 = 15 days. The figure 10 days forgets the first 5 days, and 13 1/3 days wrongly lets all 9 workers start together.
tags: ncert:CUET GAT syllabus, Quantitative Reasoning: time and work with workers joining later

rows.subject: gat
rows.body: A shopkeeper sells two articles at Rs 1,200 each, gaining 20 per cent on one and losing 20 per cent on the other. His overall result is:
rows.explanation: The cost of the first article is 1,200 / 1.20 = Rs 1,000 and of the second is 1,200 / 0.80 = Rs 1,500. Total cost is Rs 2,500 against sales of Rs 2,400, a loss of Rs 100. Equal percentages do not cancel because they apply to different cost prices, and the 4% loss is on cost, not on sales (4% of 2,400 is 96).
tags: ncert:CUET GAT syllabus, Quantitative Reasoning: profit and loss on two articles sold at the same price

rows.subject: gat
rows.body: In an election between two candidates, the winner got 55 per cent of the valid votes and won by 1,200 votes. How many valid votes were cast?
rows.explanation: The loser got 45%, so the winning margin is 55 - 45 = 10% of the valid votes. Then 10% of the votes = 1,200, so the valid votes are 12,000. The figure 6,600 is the winner's own tally (55% of 12,000), and 24,000 treats the margin as 5%.
tags: ncert:CUET GAT syllabus, Quantitative Reasoning: percentage, winning margin in an election

rows.subject: gat
rows.body: The mean of five numbers is 18. The largest number is 30 and the range is 22. What is the sum of the three numbers other than the largest and the smallest?
rows.explanation: The sum of all five numbers is 5 x 18 = 90. The range is largest minus smallest, so the smallest is 30 - 22 = 8. The middle three add up to 90 - 30 - 8 = 52. Removing only the largest leaves 60, and subtracting the range itself gives 68.
tags: ncert:CUET GAT syllabus, Statistical Data Analysis: mean and range of a small data set

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The remainder when 345 × 29 is divided by 8 is:
rows.explanation: 345 = 43 × 8 + 1, so 345 ≡ 1 (mod 8), and 29 = 3 × 8 + 5, so 29 ≡ 5 (mod 8). The remainder of a product is the product of the remainders: 1 × 5 = 5 (check: 345 × 29 = 10005 = 1250 × 8 + 5). Adding the remainders gives 6, which is the remainder of the sum 345 + 29 = 374, not of the product.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit I Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications: modulo arithmetic, remainder of a product

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: In what ratio must tea costing ₹ 60 per kg be mixed with tea costing ₹ 80 per kg so that the mixture is worth ₹ 72 per kg?
rows.explanation: By the rule of allegation, cheaper : dearer = (dearer price − mean price) : (mean price − cheaper price) = (80 − 72) : (72 − 60) = 8 : 12 = 2 : 3. Check: 2 kg at ₹ 60 and 3 kg at ₹ 80 cost 120 + 240 = ₹ 360, and 360 ÷ 5 = ₹ 72 per kg. The ratio 3 : 2 writes the two differences the wrong way round, and 1 : 1 would give a mean price of ₹ 70.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit I Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications: allegation and mixture, ratio of mixing

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A boat takes 6 hours to cover 24 km upstream and 4 hours to cover the same distance downstream. The speed of the stream is:
rows.explanation: Upstream speed = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 km/h and downstream speed = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 km/h. Speed of the stream = (downstream − upstream) ÷ 2 = (6 − 4) ÷ 2 = 1 km/h, while the speed of the boat in still water is (6 + 4) ÷ 2 = 5 km/h. Answering 2 km/h forgets to halve the difference, and 5 km/h is the boat’s own speed.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit I Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications: boats and streams, speed of the current

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: Pipe A can fill an empty tank in 12 hours and pipe B can fill it in 20 hours, while an outlet pipe C can empty the full tank in 30 hours. If all three pipes are opened together, the empty tank will be filled in:
rows.explanation: In one hour A fills 1/12, B fills 1/20 and C empties 1/30 of the tank. Net rate = 1/12 + 1/20 − 1/30 = (5 + 3 − 2)/60 = 1/10 of the tank per hour, so the tank fills in 10 hours. Ignoring the outlet gives 60/8 = 7.5 hours, and treating the outlet as another inlet gives 6 hours.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit I Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications: pipes and cisterns, filling and emptying together

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: In a 500 m race A beats B by 50 m, and in another 500 m race B beats C by 50 m. If each runner keeps a constant speed, by how many metres does A beat C in a 500 m race?
rows.explanation: When A runs 500 m, B runs 450 m; when B runs 500 m, C runs 450 m. So when B runs 450 m, C runs 450 × 450/500 = 405 m. Hence C covers only 405 m while A covers 500 m, and A wins by 500 − 405 = 95 m (the speed ratios 10 : 9 and 10 : 9 give A : C = 100 : 81, the same result). Adding the two margins to get 100 m ignores that B’s second 50 m lead is measured over 500 m, not over the 450 m it runs here.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit I Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications: races and games, beating by a distance

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body:
Consider the following statements about numerical inequalities, where a, b and c are real numbers.
(A) If a > b, then a + c > b + c for every value of c.
(B) If a > b, then ac > bc for every value of c.
(C) If a > b and c < 0, then ac < bc.
(D) If a > b > 0, then 1/a < 1/b.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: Adding the same number to both sides never changes an inequality, so (A) is true, and multiplying both sides by a negative number reverses it, so (C) is true. For positive numbers the larger one has the smaller reciprocal (2 > 1 but 1/2 < 1), so (D) is true. Statement (B) fails for c = 0 and for every negative c, which is the common slip of forgetting that the sign reverses for a negative multiplier.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit I Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications: numerical inequalities, properties of inequalities

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A is 50% more efficient than B. Working together, A and B can complete a piece of work in 12 days. How many days would B alone take to complete the work?
rows.explanation: The efficiencies of A and B are in the ratio 150 : 100 = 3 : 2, so together they do 3 + 2 = 5 units of work a day. Total work = 5 × 12 = 60 units, and B alone does 2 units a day, so B takes 60 ÷ 2 = 30 days. Check: 1/20 + 1/30 = 5/60 = 1/12. The 20 days is the time A alone would take, not B.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit I Numbers, Quantification and Numerical Applications: numerical problems, time and work with relative efficiency

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A perpetuity pays ₹ 6,000 at the end of every year for ever. If the rate of interest is 8% per annum, its present value is:
rows.explanation: The present value of a perpetuity is the payment divided by the rate of interest: 6,000 ÷ 0.08 = ₹ 75,000. Check: ₹ 75,000 invested at 8% earns exactly ₹ 6,000 a year with the capital left intact. Multiplying 6,000 by 0.08 gives ₹ 480, which is a year’s interest on the payment and not the sum needed to fund it.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit VII Financial Mathematics: perpetuity, present value of a perpetuity

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A loan of ₹ 60,000 is taken at 10% per annum flat rate for 2 years and is repaid in equal monthly instalments. The EMI under the flat rate method is:
rows.explanation: Under the flat rate method interest is charged on the original principal for the whole period: 60,000 × 10% × 2 = ₹ 12,000. Total repayment = 60,000 + 12,000 = ₹ 72,000, and spreading it over 2 × 12 = 24 months gives 72,000 ÷ 24 = ₹ 3,000. The figure ₹ 2,500 is the principal alone divided by 24, leaving out the interest.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit VII Financial Mathematics: EMI by the flat rate method

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A firm deposits an equal amount at the end of each year for 2 years in a sinking fund that earns 10% per annum compound interest, so as to have ₹ 46,200 at the end of the 2nd year. The yearly deposit is:
rows.explanation: The first deposit earns one year’s interest, so the fund after 2 years is P × 1.1 + P = 2.1P. Setting 2.1P = 46,200 gives P = ₹ 22,000; check: 22,000 × 1.1 + 22,000 = 24,200 + 22,000 = 46,200. Dividing 46,200 by 2 gives ₹ 23,100, which ignores the interest the fund earns.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit VII Financial Mathematics: sinking fund, periodic deposit

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I:
(A) Perpetuity
(B) Sinking fund
(C) Rate of return
(D) Straight-line depreciation
List-II:
(I) Gain on an investment, income plus rise in value, as a percentage of the amount invested
(II) Equal amount written off an asset’s cost in every year of its useful life
(III) Money built up by regular deposits to meet a liability on a future date
(IV) Equal payments continuing for ever at regular intervals
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: A perpetuity is a stream of equal payments with no end, a sinking fund is built from regular deposits so that a liability can be met on a fixed date, the rate of return compares income plus change in value with the sum invested, and straight-line depreciation writes off (cost − residual value) ÷ life equally each year. Linking the sinking fund with the equal yearly write-off confuses a fund that is built up with an expense that is charged.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit VII Financial Mathematics: perpetuity, sinking fund, rate of return and linear depreciation terms

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The value of a fund grows by 25% in the first year and by 80% in the second year. Its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the two years is:
rows.explanation: Over two years the value is multiplied by 1.25 × 1.80 = 2.25. CAGR is the constant yearly rate that gives this growth: (1 + g)² = 2.25, so 1 + g = 1.5 and g = 50%. Check: 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25. The average of 25% and 80% is 52.5%, and the total gain of 125% divided by 2 is 62.5%; neither is a compound rate.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit VII Financial Mathematics: compound annual growth rate versus simple annual growth rate

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A machine bought for ₹ 1,80,000 has a residual value of ₹ 30,000 and a useful life of 5 years. Using the straight-line method, its book value at the end of 2 years is:
rows.explanation: Annual depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life = (1,80,000 − 30,000) ÷ 5 = ₹ 30,000. After 2 years the total depreciation is ₹ 60,000, so the book value is 1,80,000 − 60,000 = ₹ 1,20,000. The figure ₹ 60,000 is only the depreciation charged so far, and ignoring the residual value gives ₹ 36,000 a year and a book value of 1,80,000 − 72,000 = ₹ 1,08,000.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit VII Financial Mathematics: linear (straight line) depreciation, cost, residual value and useful life

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A discrete random variable X takes the values 1, 2 and 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 respectively. The variance of X is:
rows.explanation: The mean is E(X) = 1(0.2) + 2(0.5) + 3(0.3) = 2.1 and E(X²) = 1(0.2) + 4(0.5) + 9(0.3) = 4.9. The variance is E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 4.9 − 4.41 = 0.49. The value 4.90 is E(X²) before the squared mean is subtracted, and 0.70 is the standard deviation, not the variance.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit IV Probability Distributions: variance and standard deviation of a discrete random variable

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I:
(A) Mean of a binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.4
(B) Variance of a binomial distribution with n = 12 and p = 0.5
(C) Variance of a Poisson distribution with mean 6
(D) Variance of the standard normal distribution
List-II:
(I) 3
(II) 6
(III) 1
(IV) 4
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: The binomial mean is np = 10 × 0.4 = 4 and the binomial variance is npq = 12 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 3. A Poisson distribution has variance equal to its mean, so 6, and the standard normal variate has mean 0 and variance 1. Using np = 6 for the binomial with n = 12 gives its mean rather than its variance.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit IV Probability Distributions: mean and variance of binomial, Poisson and standard normal distributions

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A Poisson variate X satisfies E(X²) = 12. The variance of X is:
rows.explanation: For a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance both equal λ, so E(X²) = variance + (mean)² = λ + λ². Then λ² + λ − 12 = 0, that is (λ + 4)(λ − 3) = 0, and since λ > 0, λ = 3 and the variance is 3. The value 12 is E(X²) itself, and 9 is λ² rather than the variance.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit IV Probability Distributions: Poisson distribution, mean and variance both equal to λ

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The heights of plants in a nursery are normally distributed with mean 40 cm and standard deviation 5 cm. Approximately what percentage of the plants have heights between 35 cm and 45 cm?
rows.explanation: The limits 35 cm and 45 cm give z = (35 − 40)/5 = −1 and z = (45 − 40)/5 = +1, so they lie within one standard deviation of the mean. About 68% of a normal distribution lies within μ ± σ. The figure 95% belongs to μ ± 2σ, which would be 30 cm to 50 cm.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit IV Probability Distributions: normal distribution, standard normal variate and the 68-95-99.7 area relationship

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The first two values of a time series are 10 and 15. Its 3-year moving averages for the second and third years are 17 and 19. The fourth value of the series is:
rows.explanation: A 3-year moving average is the mean of three consecutive values. From the second average, 3 × 17 = 51 = 10 + 15 + third value, so the third value is 26. From the third average, 3 × 19 = 57 = 15 + 26 + fourth value, so the fourth value is 16. Adding 3 × (19 − 17) = 6 to the second value gives 21, which is wrong because the first value is the one that drops out of the window.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit V Time Based Data: moving average method of measuring trend

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The annual output (in thousand units) of a firm over five consecutive years is 10, 14, 19, 20 and 22. A straight-line trend y = a + bt is fitted by the method of least squares with the middle year as origin and t = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2. The trend value for the last year (in thousand units) is:
rows.explanation: Here a = Σy/5 = 85/5 = 17 and b = Σty/Σt² = (−20 − 14 + 0 + 20 + 44)/10 = 3, so the trend line is y = 17 + 3t. For the last year t = 2, the trend value is 17 + 6 = 23. The value 22 is the observed output, not the trend value, and dividing Σty by 5 instead of Σt² gives b = 6 and the wrong value 29.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit V Time Based Data: least squares linear trend and interpreting trend values

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A list of 400 students is numbered 1 to 400. A systematic sample of 20 students is drawn by starting at the student numbered 6 and then selecting every kth student. The number of the fourth student selected is:
rows.explanation: In systematic sampling the interval is k = N/n = 400/20 = 20. Starting at 6, the selected students are numbered 6, 26, 46 and 66, so the fourth is 66. The number 46 is only the third student selected, and 80 comes from ignoring the starting point (4 × 20).
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit VI Inferential Statistics: systematic sampling, selecting every kth unit

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A sample of 16 values has mean 53 and standard deviation 4.8. To test H0: μ = 50 against H1: μ ≠ 50 at the 5% level, the table value of t for 15 degrees of freedom is 2.13. The calculated t and the decision are:
rows.explanation: The standard error is s/√n = 4.8/4 = 1.2, so t = (53 − 50)/1.2 = 2.5. This exceeds the table value 2.13, so H0 is rejected. Dividing by s instead of s/√n gives 0.625, and dividing by s/n = 0.3 gives 10; neither is the t statistic.
tags: ncert:CUET 2026 Applied Mathematics syllabus, Unit VI Inferential Statistics: one-sample t statistic and testing a null hypothesis

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The matrix [0 9 a; −9 0 7; 8 b 0] is skew-symmetric. The value of a + b is:
rows.explanation: In a skew-symmetric matrix aij = −aji and the diagonal entries are zero. Here a13 = a and a31 = 8 give a = −8, while a23 = 7 and a32 = b give b = −7, so a + b = −15. Keeping the signs equal, as in a symmetric matrix, would give a = 8 and b = 7 and the wrong sum 15.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 3 Matrices: skew-symmetric matrices, Aᵀ = −A

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: Match List-I with List-II. List-I: (A) Scalar matrix (B) Skew-symmetric matrix (C) Row matrix (D) Column matrix. List-II: (I) Aᵀ = −A (II) Order 1 × n (III) Order m × 1 (IV) Diagonal matrix with all diagonal entries equal. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are all equal, a skew-symmetric matrix satisfies Aᵀ = −A, a row matrix has a single row so its order is 1 × n, and a column matrix has a single column so its order is m × 1. Swapping the row and column matrices is the usual slip, because both have only one line of entries.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 3 Matrices: types of matrices and their defining properties

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The matrices A = [2 1; 6 3] and B = [1 k; −2 4] satisfy AB = O, the zero matrix. The value of k is:
rows.explanation: AB has first row (2 × 1 + 1 × (−2), 2 × k + 1 × 4) = (0, 2k + 4) and second row (6 × 1 + 3 × (−2), 6 × k + 3 × 4) = (0, 6k + 12). Both vanish only when k = −2. The product of two non-zero matrices can be the zero matrix because A is singular, and k = −4 comes from dropping the factor 2 in 2k + 4 = 0.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 3 Matrices: product of non-zero matrices can be the zero matrix

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The inverse of the matrix [6 5; 2 2] is:
rows.explanation: For the given matrix A, |A| = 6 × 2 − 5 × 2 = 2. The inverse is (1/|A|) × adj A, and adj A swaps the diagonal entries and changes the signs of the off-diagonal ones, so A⁻¹ = (1/2) × [2 −5; −2 6]. Leaving out the factor 1/|A| gives the adjoint itself, which is not the inverse.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 3 Matrices: inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix using the adjoint

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: For A = [1 2; 0 1] and B = [1 0; 2 1], the matrix (A + B)² − (A² + 2AB + B²) equals:
rows.explanation: Since (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², the required difference is BA − AB. Here AB = [5 2; 2 1] and BA = [1 2; 2 5], so BA − AB = [−4 0; 0 4]. The zero matrix would hold only if AB = BA, but matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 3 Matrices: non-commutativity of matrix multiplication

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body:
Consider the following statements about determinants of square matrices.
(A) Interchanging any two rows of a determinant changes its sign.
(B) |A + B| = |A| + |B| for any two square matrices A and B of the same order.
(C) If A is non-singular, then |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|.
(D) A square matrix with two identical columns is singular.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: Swapping two rows flips the sign of a determinant, |A||A⁻¹| = |I| = 1 gives |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|, and two equal columns make the determinant 0, so that matrix is singular. The sum rule is false: determinants multiply, |AB| = |A||B|, but |A + B| is not |A| + |B|; for order 2, |I + I| = 4 while |I| + |I| = 2.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 4 Determinants: properties of determinants, singular matrices and |A⁻¹|

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: For what value of k does the system of equations 2x + 3y = 5 and 4x + ky = 9 have no solution?
rows.explanation: The coefficient determinant is 2k − 12, which is zero only for k = 6. For k = 6 the second equation reads 4x + 6y = 9, while twice the first gives 4x + 6y = 10, so the two equations contradict and there is no solution. Any other k gives a non-zero determinant and a unique solution; k = 3/2 comes from inverting the ratio of coefficients.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 4 Determinants: consistency and number of solutions of a system of linear equations

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A and B are square matrices of order 3 with |A| = 3 and |B| = 2, and B is invertible. The value of |2AB⁻¹| is:
rows.explanation: For order n = 3, |kM| = k^n |M|, so |2AB⁻¹| = 2³ × |A| × |B⁻¹| = 8 × 3 × (1/2) = 12, because |B⁻¹| = 1/|B|. Taking the factor as 2 instead of 2³ gives 3, treating |B⁻¹| as |B| gives 48, and leaving out B⁻¹ altogether gives 24.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 4 Determinants: |kA| = k^n |A|, |AB| = |A||B| and the determinant of an inverse

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: Match List-I with List-II. List-I: (A) Decision variables (B) Feasible solution (C) Unbounded feasible region (D) Infeasible problem. List-II: (I) A point satisfying all the constraints and the non-negativity conditions (II) Quantities whose values are to be found to optimise the objective function (III) No point satisfies all the constraints together (IV) Region extends indefinitely in some direction. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: Decision variables are the quantities to be found to optimise the objective function, a feasible solution satisfies every constraint including non-negativity, an unbounded feasible region extends indefinitely in some direction, and an infeasible problem has no point satisfying all the constraints. Confusing a feasible solution with an infeasible problem is the common slip: the first is one valid point, the second means there is none.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 12 Linear Programming: terminology: decision variables, feasible and infeasible solutions, unbounded region

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: Which of the following points lies in the feasible region of the constraints 2x + y ≤ 10, x + 3y ≤ 15, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0?
rows.explanation: A point is feasible only if it satisfies every constraint. The point (2, 3) gives 2 × 2 + 3 = 7 ≤ 10 and 2 + 3 × 3 = 11 ≤ 15. Both (4, 3) and (5, 1) break the first constraint (11 > 10), and (2, 5) breaks the second (17 > 15), so each of them passes only one of the two checks.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 12 Linear Programming: feasible solutions and the feasible region

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A bakery makes x batches of bread and y batches of cake in a day. A batch of bread uses 3 kg of flour and a batch of cake uses 2 kg. Only 30 kg of flour is available, and at least 4 batches of bread must be made. Besides x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, the constraints are:
rows.explanation: The flour used, 3x + 2y, cannot exceed the 30 kg available, so 3x + 2y ≤ 30. The phrase "at least 4 batches of bread" is a lower limit, so x ≥ 4. Writing 3x + 2y ≥ 30 reverses the resource limit, and x ≤ 4 reverses the minimum requirement; 2x + 3y swaps the flour used per batch.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 12 Linear Programming: mathematical formulation of a linear programming problem from words

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: To minimise its cost Z = 5x + 2y (in rupees), a firm must satisfy 2x + y ≥ 8, x + 2y ≥ 10, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. The least possible cost is:
rows.explanation: The feasible region is unbounded, but Z has positive coefficients, so a minimum exists and lies at a corner point. The corners are (0, 8), (2, 4) and (10, 0), where Z = 16, 18 and 50, so the minimum is 16. The value 18 comes from using only the intersection of the two lines and ignoring the corner on the y-axis.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 12 Linear Programming: corner point method on an unbounded feasible region

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: How many corner points does the region defined by 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, 0 ≤ y ≤ 4, x + y ≤ 6 and x + 2y ≤ 20 have?
rows.explanation: The lines x + y = 6, x = 4 and y = 4 with the two axes enclose a region with corner points (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 2), (2, 4) and (0, 4), so there are 5. The inequality x + 2y ≤ 20 holds at all of them (its largest value is 10 at (2, 4)), so it cuts nothing off; counting every inequality that is written (6 in all) would give 6.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 12 Linear Programming: feasible region, corner points and a redundant constraint

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The number of reflexive relations that can be defined on a set containing 3 elements is:
rows.explanation: A reflexive relation on a 3-element set must contain the 3 pairs (a, a), while each of the other 3 × 3 − 3 = 6 ordered pairs may be included or left out freely. So there are 2^6 = 64 reflexive relations. The value 512 = 2^9 counts every relation on the set, and 8 = 2^3 wrongly counts choices on the three pairs that are compulsory.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 1 Relations and Functions: reflexive relations on a small finite set

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The curve x² + xy + y² = 7 passes through the point (1, 2). For this curve, dy/dx at (1, 2) equals:
rows.explanation: Differentiate both sides with respect to x, applying the product rule to xy: 2x + y + x(dy/dx) + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y). At (1, 2) this is −(2 + 2)/(1 + 4) = −4/5. Dropping the y that the product rule produces gives −2/5, and inverting the fraction gives −5/4.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 5 Continuity and Differentiability: derivative of implicit functions

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A curve is given parametrically by x = t² and y = t³, where t is a real parameter. The second derivative d²y/dx² at t = 2 equals:
rows.explanation: Here dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 3t²/2t = 3t/2. Then d²y/dx² = [d/dt(3t/2)]/(dx/dt) = (3/2)/(2t) = 3/(4t), which is 3/8 at t = 2. Stopping at d/dt(3t/2) gives 3/2, and dividing d²y/dt² by dx/dt gives 12/4 = 3.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 5 Continuity and Differentiability: parametric differentiation and second order derivatives

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I (function)
(A) e^(3x)
(B) log_e (3x)
(C) tan⁻¹(3x)
(D) sin⁻¹ x
List-II (derivative with respect to x)
(I) 1/x
(II) 3/(1 + 9x²)
(III) 1/√(1 − x²)
(IV) 3e^(3x)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
rows.explanation: By the chain rule, d/dx e^(3x) = 3e^(3x), d/dx log_e (3x) = 3/(3x) = 1/x and d/dx tan⁻¹(3x) = 3/(1 + 9x²), while d/dx sin⁻¹ x = 1/√(1 − x²). The factor 3 from the inner function survives in the exponential and in the tan⁻¹ result but cancels in the logarithm.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 5 Continuity and Differentiability: derivatives of exponential, logarithmic and inverse trigonometric functions

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The function f(x) = x² − 2 log_e x, with domain x > 0, is strictly increasing on which of the following intervals?
rows.explanation: f′(x) = 2x − 2/x = 2(x² − 1)/x. For x > 0 the sign of f′ is the sign of x² − 1, which is positive only when x > 1, so f increases on (1, ∞). On (0, 1) the derivative is negative, so that is where f decreases; (0, ∞) wrongly treats x² as the only term.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part I, Ch 6 Application of Derivatives: increasing and decreasing functions

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: Suppose f is an integrable function on [0, 4] such that ∫ from 0 to 4 of f(x) dx = 7 and ∫ from 2 to 4 of f(x) dx = 3. Then ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2f(x) + 1) dx is equal to:
rows.explanation: By additivity, ∫ from 0 to 2 of f(x) dx = 7 − 3 = 4. Then ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2f(x) + 1) dx = 2(4) + [x] from 0 to 2 = 8 + 2 = 10. Treating the integral of the constant 1 over [0, 2] as 1 instead of 2 gives 9, and adding 7 and 3 instead of subtracting gives 22.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 7 Integrals: properties of definite integrals (additivity and linearity)

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The integral of x log_e x with respect to x, taken from 1 to e, equals:
rows.explanation: Integrating by parts with u = log_e x and dv = x dx gives (x²/2) log_e x − x²/4. At x = e this is e²/2 − e²/4 = e²/4, and at x = 1 it is −1/4, so the value is e²/4 + 1/4 = (e² + 1)/4. Subtracting 1/4 instead of adding it gives (e² − 1)/4.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 7 Integrals: integration by parts and evaluation of a definite integral

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: Find the area lying under the curve y = x² + 2 between the vertical lines x = 1 and x = 4.
rows.explanation: Area = ∫ from 1 to 4 of (x² + 2) dx = [x³/3 + 2x] from 1 to 4 = (64/3 + 8) − (1/3 + 2) = 21 + 6 = 27. Leaving out the 2x term gives only 21, and forgetting to divide x³ by 3 gives 69.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 8 Application of Integrals: area under a curve between two ordinates

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The parabola y = 4x − x² cuts the x-axis at two points. The area between the parabola and the x-axis is:
rows.explanation: The parabola meets the x-axis where 4x − x² = 0, that is at x = 0 and x = 4, and lies above the axis between them. Area = ∫ from 0 to 4 of (4x − x²) dx = [2x² − x³/3] from 0 to 4 = 32 − 64/3 = 32/3. Integrating only 4x gives 32, which ignores the −x² term.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 8 Application of Integrals: area between a parabola and the x-axis

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The area of the region bounded by y = x³, the x-axis and the ordinates x = −1 and x = 2 equals:
rows.explanation: The curve lies below the x-axis for −1 < x < 0 and above it for 0 < x < 2, so the two parts are added as positive areas: ∫ from −1 to 0 of |x³| dx = 1/4 and ∫ from 0 to 2 of x³ dx = 4, giving 17/4. The single integral from −1 to 2 gives 15/4, which lets the negative part cancel instead of adding.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 8 Application of Integrals: area under a curve when the curve crosses the axis

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: If y = y(x) satisfies dy/dx = (x + y)/x for x > 0 with y(1) = 2, then y(e) equals:
rows.explanation: Put y = vx, so v + x(dv/dx) = 1 + v and dv = dx/x, giving v = log_e x + C and y = x log_e x + Cx. The condition y(1) = 2 gives C = 2, so y(e) = e(1 + 2) = 3e. Writing y = x log_e x + 2 loses the factor x on the constant and gives e + 2.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 9 Differential Equations: homogeneous equations of first order and first degree

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Eliminating the constant A from y = Ax² gives the differential equation x(dy/dx) = 2y.
(B) The equation dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy) is homogeneous.
(C) The equation dy/dx = y/x has the solution y = x + C, where C is a constant.
(D) Separating the variables in dy/dx = x/y leads to y² − x² = C.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
rows.explanation: From y = Ax², dy/dx = 2Ax = 2y/x, so x(dy/dx) = 2y and (A) is true. Scaling x and y by the same factor leaves (x² + y²)/(xy) unchanged, so (B) is true. Separating dy/y = dx/x gives y = Cx, not y = x + C, so (C) is false. Separating y dy = x dx gives y² = x² + 2K, which is y² − x² = C, so (D) is true.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 9 Differential Equations: forming an equation from a family of curves, homogeneous equations and variable separable solutions

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The diagonals of a parallelogram are represented by the vectors i + 2j + 2k and 3i − 2j + 2k. The area of the parallelogram, in square units, is:
rows.explanation: The cross product of the diagonals is (8, 4, −8), with magnitude √(64 + 16 + 64) = 12. The parallelogram has half this area, 12/2 = 6. Using 12 forgets the half, and 3√17/2 is half the product of the diagonal lengths, valid only when the diagonals are perpendicular.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 10 Vector Algebra: vector (cross) product and area of a parallelogram with given diagonals

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I
(A) Non-zero vectors a and b are perpendicular
(B) Non-zero vectors a and b are parallel
(C) Area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b
(D) Unit vector in the direction of a
List-II
(I) |a × b|
(II) a · b = 0
(III) a/|a|
(IV) a × b = 0
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
rows.explanation: Perpendicular vectors have a zero dot product, a · b = 0, while parallel vectors have a zero cross product, a × b = 0. The magnitude |a × b| is the area of the parallelogram on a and b, and a/|a| is the unit vector along a. Swapping the dot and cross conditions is the usual mistake.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 10 Vector Algebra: dot product, cross product and unit vector

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: The lines (x − 1)/4 = (y + 2)/k = (z − 3)/2 and (x + 3)/3 = (y − 1)/(−2) = (z + 5)/(−1) are perpendicular to each other. The value of k is:
rows.explanation: The direction ratios are (4, k, 2) and (3, −2, −1). Perpendicular lines have a zero dot product, so 4(3) + k(−2) + 2(−1) = 12 − 2k − 2 = 0, giving k = 5. A sign slip on the last term gives 7, and ignoring the third components gives 6.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 11 Three Dimensional Geometry: direction ratios and perpendicular lines

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: A straight line passes through the points (−2, 1, 5) and (0, 4, 9). The z-coordinate of the point on this line whose x-coordinate is 4 is:
rows.explanation: The direction ratios are (0 + 2, 4 − 1, 9 − 5) = (2, 3, 4), so a general point is (−2 + 2t, 1 + 3t, 5 + 4t). Putting x = 4 gives −2 + 2t = 4, so t = 3 and z = 5 + 12 = 17. Treating the starting x as +2 gives t = 1 and z = 9, while taking t = x/2 = 2 gives 13.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 11 Three Dimensional Geometry: Cartesian equation of a line through two points

rows.subject: mathematics
rows.body: Three machines A, B and C produce 50%, 30% and 20% of the items in a factory. Of their items, 2%, 5% and 10% respectively are defective. An item chosen at random is found to be defective. The probability that machine B made it is:
rows.explanation: By total probability, P(defective) = 0.5 × 0.02 + 0.3 × 0.05 + 0.2 × 0.10 = 0.010 + 0.015 + 0.020 = 0.045. By Bayes theorem, P(B | defective) = 0.015/0.045 = 1/3. The value 3/10 is only the share of output from B, ignoring the evidence, and 4/9 is the corresponding value for C.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Part II, Ch 13 Probability: total probability theorem and Bayes theorem

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A galvanometer of resistance 99 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 10 mA. It is converted into an ammeter of range 0 to 1 A by connecting a shunt. The resistance of the ammeter so formed is:
rows.explanation: For the shunt, Ig × G = (I − Ig) × S, so S = (0.010 × 99)/(1 − 0.010) = 1.0 Ω. The shunt is in parallel with the galvanometer, so the ammeter resistance is G S/(G + S) = 99 × 1.0/100 = 0.99 Ω, which also equals Ig G/I = 0.99/1. Quoting 1.0 Ω gives only the shunt, 100 Ω adds the two resistances as if in series, and 99 Ω ignores the shunt altogether.
tags: unit:Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 4 Moving Charges and Magnetism: moving coil galvanometer, conversion to an ammeter with a shunt and the resulting resistance
rows.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A beam of singly charged ions enters a region where a uniform electric field of 3.0 × 10^4 V/m and a uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T act at right angles to each other and to the beam. Ions of which speed pass through undeflected?
rows.explanation: Ions pass undeflected when the electric and magnetic forces balance, qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 3.0 × 10^4 / 0.10 = 3.0 × 10^5 m/s. The charge and the mass cancel, so every singly charged ion with this speed goes straight. The product E × B = 3.0 × 10^3 has the wrong dimensions for a speed.
tags: unit:Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 4 Moving Charges and Magnetism: motion of a charge in combined electric and magnetic fields (velocity selector)
rows.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: An electron moves in a circular orbit of radius 5.0 × 10^-11 m with a speed of 3.0 × 10^6 m/s. Take e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C. The magnetic moment due to this orbital motion is:
rows.explanation: One revolution takes T = 2πr/v, so the equivalent current is I = e/T = ev/(2πr). The magnetic moment is m = I × πr² = evr/2 = (1.6 × 10^-19)(3.0 × 10^6)(5.0 × 10^-11)/2 = 1.2 × 10^-23 A m². Leaving out the factor 1/2 gives 2.4 × 10^-23 A m², which is the value of evr, and 4.8 × 10^-23 doubles it.
tags: unit:Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 4 Moving Charges and Magnetism: current loop as a magnetic dipole, magnetic moment of a revolving electron
rows.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: Two long straight parallel wires are 0.40 m apart and carry steady currents of 3 A and 5 A in opposite directions. On the straight line through both wires, the net magnetic field is zero at a distance from the 3 A wire of:
rows.explanation: For opposite currents the two fields add between the wires, so a null point can only lie outside them, beyond the weaker (3 A) wire. With x measured from the 3 A wire, μ0(3)/(2πx) = μ0(5)/(2π(x + 0.40)), so 3(x + 0.40) = 5x and x = 0.60 m. The value 0.15 m is the null point for currents in the same direction, and 1.0 m is the distance of the correct point from the 5 A wire.
tags: unit:Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 4 Moving Charges and Magnetism: magnetic field of a long straight current-carrying wire and superposition
rows.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism

rows.subject: physics
rows.body:
Consider the following statements about electromagnetic induction.
(A) The emf induced in a closed loop depends on the resistance of the loop.
(B) An emf can be induced in a coil placed in a steady magnetic field by changing the area of the coil.
(C) One henry is equal to one weber per ampere.
(D) A metal rod at rest in a steady magnetic field has a motional emf between its ends.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: Induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux, and the resistance of the loop only decides the current, so statement (A) fails. Changing the area changes the flux and induces an emf, and since L = flux/current, 1 H = 1 Wb/A. A rod at rest has v = 0, so its motional emf Blv is zero even in a steady field.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 6 Electromagnetic Induction: Faraday law, motional emf and the unit of inductance

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A coil of 100 turns and resistance 20 Ω is linked with a flux that falls from 4.0 × 10^-3 Wb to 1.0 × 10^-3 Wb through each turn in 0.50 s. The total charge that flows through the coil is:
rows.explanation: The charge is q = NΔΦ/R = 100 × (4.0 − 1.0) × 10^-3 / 20 = 1.5 × 10^-2 C, independent of the time taken. Check: emf = 0.30/0.50 = 0.60 V, current = 0.60/20 = 0.030 A, charge = 0.030 × 0.50 = 1.5 × 10^-2 C. The value 3.0 × 10^-2 is the current in amperes, not the charge.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 6 Electromagnetic Induction: induced emf, current and the charge that flows through a coil

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A square coil of side 10 cm and 100 turns is placed with its plane making an angle of 30° with a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. The field is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.010 s. The magnitude of the induced emf is:
rows.explanation: The field makes 30° with the plane, so it makes 60° with the normal and the flux per turn is BA cos 60° = 0.20 × 0.010 × 0.5 = 1.0 × 10^-3 Wb. Then ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 1.0 × 10^-3 / 0.010 = 10 V. Using cos 30° treats the given angle as the one with the normal and gives 10√3 V, while taking the field as perpendicular gives 20 V.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 6 Electromagnetic Induction: magnetic flux through a tilted coil and Faraday law

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A lamp rated 100 W at 100 V is to be operated from a 125 V AC supply, with a pure inductor connected in series so that the lamp works at its rated power. The inductive reactance of the inductor must be:
rows.explanation: The lamp resistance is R = V²/P = 100²/100 = 100 Ω and its rated current is 100/100 = 1 A. The circuit must have Z = 125/1 = 125 Ω, so X_L = √(Z² − R²) = √(125² − 100²) = 75 Ω. Subtracting the resistances gives 25 Ω, but resistance and reactance combine at right angles, and adding the squares instead of subtracting them gives 160 Ω.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 7 Alternating Current: resistance and reactance in series, impedance Z = √(R² + X²)

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A series LCR circuit is connected to a 100 V (rms) AC source. The resistance is 30 Ω, the inductive reactance is 80 Ω and the capacitive reactance is 40 Ω. The rms voltage across the inductor is:
rows.explanation: The impedance is Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²) = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, so I = 100/50 = 2 A and VL = I × XL = 2 × 80 = 160 V. This is larger than the supply because VL and VC are in antiphase: the phasor sum is √(60² + (160 − 80)²) = 100 V. Taking 100 V assumes no part can exceed the source, which holds only for in-phase voltages.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 7 Alternating Current: series LCR circuit, phasors, impedance and component voltages

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: The emf of an AC generator varies as e = e0 sin ωt and the frequency is 50 Hz. Starting from e = 0, the time taken for the emf to first reach half of its peak value e0 is:
rows.explanation: When e = e0/2, sin ωt = 1/2, so ωt = π/6. With ω = 2π × 50 = 100π rad/s, t = (π/6)/(100π) = 1/600 s. A time of 1/300 s corresponds to ωt = π/3 (the sine of 60°), 1/200 s is the quarter period needed to reach the peak, and 1/100 s is the half period.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 7 Alternating Current: AC generator, instantaneous emf e = e0 sin ωt

rows.subject: physics
rows.body:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (A) Radio waves (B) Infrared waves (C) X-rays (D) Gamma rays
List-II: (I) High-energy electrons striking a metal target (II) Transitions of excited atomic nuclei (III) Rapid acceleration and deceleration of electrons in an aerial (IV) Vibrations of atoms and molecules in hot bodies
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: Radio waves come from rapid acceleration and deceleration of electrons in an aerial, infrared from vibrating atoms and molecules in hot bodies, X-rays from high-energy electrons striking a metal target, and gamma rays from excited nuclei. A common slip is to swap X-rays and gamma rays, which differ in origin: electron collisions with matter against nuclear transitions.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 8 Electromagnetic Waves: sources of the electromagnetic spectrum

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: The magnetic field amplitude of a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum is 2.0 × 10^-7 T. Take c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s. The amplitude of its electric field is:
rows.explanation: In vacuum the amplitudes of an electromagnetic wave are related by E0/B0 = c, so E0 = cB0 = 3.0 × 10^8 × 2.0 × 10^-7 = 60 V/m. Dividing B0 by c gives 6.7 × 10^-16, which inverts the relation, and multiplying by c twice overshoots to 1.8 × 10^10.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 8 Electromagnetic Waves: characteristics of electromagnetic waves, E0/B0 = c

rows.subject: physics
rows.body:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (A) Silicon doped with arsenic (B) Silicon doped with indium (C) p-n junction under forward bias (D) p-n junction under reverse bias
List-II: (I) Holes are the majority carriers (II) Narrow depletion layer and large current (III) Electrons are the majority carriers (IV) Wide depletion layer and very small current
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: Arsenic has five valence electrons and makes silicon n-type, with electrons as the majority carriers; indium has three and makes it p-type, with holes as the majority carriers. Forward bias narrows the depletion layer and gives a large current, whereas reverse bias widens it and gives only a very small current. Swapping the two dopants is the common slip.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics: n-type and p-type doping, p-n junction under forward and reverse bias

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: In a doped silicon sample the electron concentration is 4.0 × 10^22 m^-3. The intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon is 2.0 × 10^16 m^-3. The hole concentration in the sample is:
rows.explanation: In a doped semiconductor n_e × n_h = n_i². So n_h = (2.0 × 10^16)² / (4.0 × 10^22) = 4.0 × 10^32 / 4.0 × 10^22 = 1.0 × 10^10 m^-3. Donor doping raises the electrons and suppresses the holes far below n_i, so keeping the value n_i is wrong, as is multiplying n_e by n_i.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics: intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, n_e n_h = n_i²

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A silicon diode, which drops 0.7 V when it conducts, is connected in the forward direction in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor and a 5.7 V battery. The current in the circuit is:
rows.explanation: A conducting silicon diode drops 0.7 V, so the resistor has 5.7 − 0.7 = 5.0 V across it and I = 5.0/1000 = 5.0 mA. Check: 5.0 mA × 1.0 kΩ + 0.7 V = 5.7 V. Ignoring the diode drop gives 5.7 mA, while subtracting 0.7 twice gives 4.3 mA.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics: p-n junction diode in forward bias, forward voltage drop

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A pebble lies at the bottom of a pool of water (refractive index 4/3) that is 2.4 m deep. Seen from directly above, the pebble appears to be raised by:
rows.explanation: For near-normal viewing the apparent depth is real depth/μ = 2.4/(4/3) = 1.8 m, so the pebble appears raised by 2.4 − 1.8 = 0.6 m. The value 1.8 m is the apparent depth itself, not the shift, and 0.8 m comes from wrongly using d(μ − 1) for the shift.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: refraction at a plane surface and the apparent depth of an object under water

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A point object is placed on the axis in air, 60 cm in front of a convex spherical glass surface (μ = 1.5) of radius of curvature 15 cm. The distance of the image from the surface is:
rows.explanation: For refraction at a single spherical surface, μ2/v − μ1/u = (μ2 − μ1)/R. With u = −60 cm and R = +15 cm, 1.5/v + 1/60 = 0.5/15 = 1/30, so 1.5/v = 1/60 and v = +90 cm, a real image inside the glass. Writing 1/v in place of 1.5/v, as for a lens, gives the tempting 60 cm.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: refraction at a spherical surface

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1.0 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5.0 cm, and its tube length (distance between the inner focal points) is 20 cm. For the final image at infinity, the magnifying power is (D = 25 cm):
rows.explanation: With the final image at infinity, M = (L/fₒ)(D/fₑ) = (20/1.0)(25/5.0) = 20 × 5 = 100. The factor (1 + D/fₑ) = 6 gives 120, but that belongs to a final image at the near point, and 130 comes from using the 26 cm lens separation as if it were the tube length.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: compound microscope, tube length and magnifying power

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: Two thin prisms are joined with their refracting edges pointing in opposite directions. One has angle 6° and refractive index 1.5; the other has angle 4° and refractive index 1.6. The net deviation of a ray passing through the combination is:
rows.explanation: A thin prism deviates a ray by δ = (μ − 1)A, giving 0.5 × 6° = 3.0° and 0.6 × 4° = 2.4°. The prisms are inverted relative to each other, so the deviations subtract: 3.0° − 2.4° = 0.6°. Adding them gives 5.4°, and using μA instead of (μ − 1)A gives 2.6°.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: refraction through a thin prism, deviation δ = (μ − 1)A

rows.subject: physics
rows.body:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I: (A) Signal transmission through an optical fibre (B) Image formation by a convex lens (C) Image formation by a plane mirror (D) Splitting of white light by a glass prism
List-II: (I) Reflection (II) Total internal reflection (III) Dispersion (IV) Refraction
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: An optical fibre guides light by repeated total internal reflection, a convex lens forms its image by refraction at its two surfaces, a plane mirror forms its image by reflection, and a prism spreads white light into colours by dispersion because the refractive index varies with wavelength. Pairing the prism with refraction is tempting since the light bends at its faces, but the colour spread is specifically dispersion.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 9 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: reflection, refraction, total internal reflection (optical fibres) and dispersion as the principles of optical devices

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A point source of light is placed at the principal focus of a thin convex lens. The wavefront of the light emerging from the lens is:
rows.explanation: Rays from a source at the focus leave the lens parallel to the principal axis, and wavefronts are perpendicular to the rays, so the emerging wavefront is plane. A diverging spherical wavefront is what the source itself emits before the lens, while a converging one forms when a parallel beam enters the lens.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 10 Wave Optics: wavefronts and Huygens principle, wavefront shape after a lens

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A plane wavefront travelling in air meets the surface of a transparent medium at an angle of incidence of 60°. The speed of light in the medium is c/√3. The angle of refraction is:
rows.explanation: In Huygens’ construction the wavefront turns because its speed changes: sin i / sin r = v1/v2 = c/(c/√3) = √3. So sin r = sin 60°/√3 = (√3/2)/√3 = 1/2 and r = 30°. Dividing the angle itself, 60°/√3 ≈ 35°, treats the angle as proportional to the speed ratio, which Snell’s law does not.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 10 Wave Optics: refraction of a plane wave at a plane surface using Huygens principle

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on two narrow slits 0.6 mm apart, and the fringes are viewed on a screen 1.5 m away. On one side of the central maximum, the third dark fringe lies at what distance from the centre?
rows.explanation: The fringe width is β = λD/d = (400 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5)/(0.6 × 10⁻³) = 1.0 mm. Dark fringes lie at (n − ½)β from the centre, so the third (n = 3) is at 2.5β = 2.5 mm. The distance 3.0 mm marks the third bright fringe, which sits beyond the dark fringe.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 10 Wave Optics: Young’s double-slit experiment, positions of dark fringes and fringe width

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A neutron of mass 1.65 × 10^-27 kg moves with a speed of 4.0 × 10^3 m s^-1. Taking h = 6.6 × 10^-34 J s, its de Broglie wavelength is:
rows.explanation: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p = h/(mv). Here p = 1.65 × 10^-27 × 4.0 × 10^3 = 6.6 × 10^-24 kg m s^-1, so λ = 6.6 × 10^-34 / 6.6 × 10^-24 = 1.0 × 10^-10 m. Treating the momentum as mv² instead of mv would give about 2.5 × 10^-14 m.
tags: unit:Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 11 Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter: matter waves and the de Broglie relation λ = h/mv
rows.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A lamp radiates 3.3 W of monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm. Taking h = 6.6 × 10^-34 J s and c = 3.0 × 10^8 m s^-1, the number of photons emitted per second is about:
rows.explanation: The energy of one photon is E = hc/λ = (6.6 × 10^-34 × 3.0 × 10^8)/(6.0 × 10^-7) = 3.3 × 10^-19 J. The number emitted per second is N = P/E = 3.3/(3.3 × 10^-19) = 1.0 × 10^19. Writing 600 nm as 6 × 10^-6 m instead of 6 × 10^-7 m gives 1.0 × 10^20.

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: For a photosensitive metal, the stopping potential is V0 for light of wavelength λ and 3V0 for light of wavelength λ/2. The threshold wavelength of the metal is:
rows.explanation: Einstein’s equation gives eV0 = hc/λ − φ and 3eV0 = 2hc/λ − φ. Subtracting, hc/λ = 2eV0, so φ = hc/λ − eV0 = eV0 = hc/(2λ), and the threshold wavelength is hc/φ = 2λ. Reading the 3 : 1 ratio of stopping potentials as a ratio of wavelengths gives 3λ, which ignores the work function.
tags: unit:Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation

rows.body:
Match List-I (quantity for the nth Bohr orbit of hydrogen) with List-II (dependence on n).
List-I: (A) Radius of the orbit (B) Speed of the electron (C) Magnitude of the total energy (D) Angular momentum of the electron
List-II: (I) Proportional to 1/n² (II) Proportional to n (III) Proportional to 1/n (IV) Proportional to n²
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
rows.explanation: In the Bohr model the radius varies as n², the speed as 1/n, the total energy as −13.6 eV/n² so its magnitude varies as 1/n², and the angular momentum is nh/2π, proportional to n. A student who pairs the speed with 1/n² has carried the energy dependence across, since speed falls only as 1/n.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 12 Atoms: Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, radius, speed, energy and angular momentum of the nth orbit

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: An alpha particle of kinetic energy 7.2 MeV approaches a tin nucleus (atomic number 50) head-on. Taking e²/(4πε₀) = 1.44 MeV fm, the distance of closest approach is:
rows.explanation: At the closest approach all the kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy: K = (2e)(Ze)/(4πε₀r₀), so r₀ = 2Z × 1.44 MeV fm / K = (2 × 50 × 1.44)/7.2 = 20 fm. Leaving out the charge 2e of the alpha particle gives 10 fm.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 12 Atoms: alpha-particle scattering, Rutherford model and the distance of closest approach

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A sample of hydrogen atoms has all its electrons excited to the n = 4 level. The maximum number of different spectral lines that can be emitted as the atoms return to lower levels is:
rows.explanation: Spectral lines arise from transitions between pairs of levels, and four levels give n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6 pairs: 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1. Counting only the three drops from n = 4 (n − 1) misses the lines from the intermediate cascades.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 12 Atoms: energy level transitions and hydrogen line spectra

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: In the hydrogen spectrum, the ratio of the longest wavelength of the Balmer series to the shortest wavelength of the Paschen series is:
rows.explanation: With E_n = −13.6/n² eV and wavelength inversely proportional to the photon energy, the longest Balmer wavelength comes from n = 3 to n = 2: ΔE = 13.6 (1/4 − 1/9) = 13.6 × 5/36 eV, and the shortest Paschen wavelength from n = ∞ to n = 3: ΔE = 13.6/9 eV. The wavelength ratio is (1/9)/(5/36) = 4/5, so 4 : 5. Comparing the two series limits (ΔE = 13.6/4 against 13.6/9) instead gives 4 : 9.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 12 Atoms: hydrogen line spectra, Balmer and Paschen series and the Rydberg formula

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: Which one of the following pairs of nuclides consists of isotones?
rows.explanation: Isotones have the same number of neutrons, N = A − Z. C-13 has 13 − 6 = 7 neutrons and N-14 has 14 − 7 = 7. H-3 and He-3 share the mass number (isobars), C-12 and C-14 share the atomic number (isotopes), and N-14 and O-16 have 7 and 8 neutrons respectively.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 13 Nuclei: composition of the nucleus, isotopes, isobars and isotones

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: A nuclear reactor delivers 3.2 MW of power from the fission of uranium, each fission releasing 200 MeV. Taking 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10^-13 J, the number of fissions per second is:
rows.explanation: The energy per fission is 200 × 1.6 × 10^-13 = 3.2 × 10^-11 J. The fission rate is P/E = 3.2 × 10^6 / 3.2 × 10^-11 = 1.0 × 10^17 per second. Treating the energy as 200 eV instead of 200 MeV (a factor of 10^6) would give 1.0 × 10^23.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 13 Nuclei: nuclear fission and the energy released per fission

rows.subject: physics
rows.body: The binding energy per nucleon is 1.1 MeV for deuterium (H-2) and 7.1 MeV for helium (He-4). The energy released when two deuterium nuclei fuse to form one helium nucleus is:
rows.explanation: The energy released equals the binding energy of the product minus that of the reactants. He-4 has 4 × 7.1 = 28.4 MeV and the two H-2 nuclei have 2 × (2 × 1.1) = 4.4 MeV, so Q = 28.4 − 4.4 = 24.0 MeV. Subtracting the per-nucleon values (6.0 MeV) ignores the number of nucleons, and quoting 28.4 MeV forgets that the deuterons were already bound.
tags: ncert:NCERT Class 12 Physics Part II, Ch 13 Nuclei: binding energy, nuclear fusion and energy released
